episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Repair Culture & Practical Tech
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Repair Culture & Practical Tech.

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [Business Insider] Europe's biggest tech giant slides 5% on reports of a Chinese rival encroaching on its turf and [Kottke.org] How the Words We Teach English Language Learners..., plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: When building off-grid power systems, is resilience better achieved through open, repairable components or by accepting manufacturer lock-in and hoping supply chains hold? Topics include: US inverter import ban and its effect on Canadian off-grid homestead costs, Open-source mesh networks (Meshtastic) as an import-ban-resistant alternative for rural connectivity, Documentation and knowledge transfer as repair-culture solutions (wiring diagrams, monitoring logs), Offline-first device design versus cloud-dependent 'smart' systems, Distinction between informal community problem-solving and formally accountable capacity-building institutions.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Literacy Quesnel Society

discussion.central_question: When building off-grid power systems, is resilience better achieved through open, repairable components or by accepting manufacturer lock-in and hoping supply chains hold?
discussion.riley_position: Open-source design patterns like Meshtastic create import-ban-proof systems by eliminating single chokepoints, and this philosophy can transfer to power systems through documentation and monitoring practices that don't depend on any single vendor.
riley_key_evidence: Meshtastic's waterproof mesh radio nodes use generic parts from multiple suppliers, making them immune to import restrictions on any single manufacturer
Off-grid systems in the Cariboo have historically relied on salvaged and adapted parts (old alternators, decommissioned RV inverters), proving informal used-parts economies already work
Screenshotting monitoring dashboards and keeping paper logbooks costs nothing but time and outlives any single owner or installer
discussion.casey_position: The inverter market is genuinely consolidated among a handful of manufacturers (Victron, Outback, Schneider), so an import ban removes affordable competition rather than breaking open chokepoints; real durability requires formal accountability structures, not just Saturday projects.
casey_key_evidence: Import bans protecting three domestic inverter makers from cheaper competitors consolidate chokepoints instead of breaking them open, the opposite of healthy competition
Xatśūll First Nation's community-maintained digital infrastructure required formal accountability to the community over time, not casual neighbor coordination
Some 'smart' inverters require manufacturer server accounts to report your own battery voltage, creating lock-in that offline-first design can prevent
discussion.resolution: They converged on a practical filter both could endorse: before any purchase, ask whether a device works without subscriptions, accounts, or factory repair dependency—and whether neighbors can diagnose failures with a multimeter and printed manual. Riley acknowledged Casey's distinction between a weekend project and durable institutional capacity; Casey acknowledged both scales can coexist without negating each other.
